problem: Prior RL social-navigation methods (CADRL, SA-CADRL, SARL) feed pedestrian positions and are tested in open spaces with no sensing of static constraints. Classical planners (ROS navigation stack) suffer from the freezing-robot problem in dense scenes. Neither handles pedestrian interaction in constrained indoor geometry such as corridors, doorways and intersections, where space limits maneuverability and shapes pedestrian flow.
motivation: Robots in buildings and homes must pass pedestrians in tight spaces, and these spaces create layout-dependent interaction patterns. The authors observe that built environments are compositions of a few canonical templates (hallways, door exits, crosswalks, rooms). This suggests that a policy trained on a small set of simple canonical layouts might generalize to complex unseen layouts and even to real 3D scans.
key_idea: A global motion planner supplies waypoints along a shortest path, and a SAC-trained lidar-based RL policy handles local pedestrian interactions; the policy is trained on a few simple 'walls-world' layouts under a compositional multi-layout regime so it transfers to more complex compositional layouts and to real-scan meshes.
insight: Generalization depends on whether the training layouts contain the right geometric elements, not simply on how much varied experience the policy gets. On the most compositional test layout WALLS-H, ΠT1 (corridor + door exit + crosswalk) reaches 96% SR. ΠT4, which lacks the door and crosswalk layouts, drops to 78%, and single-layout Π_WALLS-F drops to 70% (Tables I–II). Training directly on a single 3D mesh overfits: the MESH-HOME-trained policy gets 84% at home but only 64% on WALLS-H, and the MESH-MARKET-trained policy gets 43.33% on MESH-HOME. The walls-trained ΠT1 stays more consistent (77/66/96). Against ROS-NAV, the RL component removes freezing: ROS-NAV timeouts rise to 35% with 16 pedestrians while ΠT1 has 0% timeouts, and its failures are collisions instead (Table IV). Input ablations (lidar frame stacking, odometry, pedestrian coordinates, time-to-collision) gave no significant gain, but no numbers are reported.
method: Hierarchical plan+learn: a sampling-based/shortest-path global planner is queried once per episode on a 2D map of static elements; n=6 waypoints (1.0 m resolution, 0.5 m tolerance) along the collision-free path are updated as the robot progresses and fed to the policy.

POMDP policy π(a|o): observation = goal (2D polar coords in robot frame) + 128-beam 1D LiDAR + 6 waypoints; output = continuous linear/angular velocity (linear [-0.2,1] m/s allowing backing up, angular [-0.5,0.5] rad/s, 0.25 s action step) for a differential-drive robot, passed to a low-level wheel velocity controller.
Reward: R_goal=+1 (within 0.5 m), R_timestep=-0.001, R_collision=-1 with episode termination, dense R_potential on distance to the next waypoint, plus R_waypoint for reaching waypoints.
Training: Soft Actor-Critic (TF-Agents) with actor and critic sharing a featurizing head; 200k training steps, 4 parallel envs, Adam, lr 3e-4, γ=0.99, replay buffer 150k, max 500 steps per episode.

Multi-agent simulation: iGibson/PyBullet with ORCA-driven pedestrians (radius 30 cm, 2 m/s, personal space 10 cm, robot visible to ORCA). Start/goal areas per layout are constrained so that ORCA trajectories are feasible.

Compositional multi-layout training: each episode samples one of several canonical 20m×20m WALLS layouts (e.g., T1 = corridor A + door exit B + crosswalk F; T2/T3/T4 drop crosswalk, door, or both). Policies are tested on unseen composed layouts WALLS-G/H/I and on Gibson 3D scans MESH-MARKET and MESH-HOME.

setting.backbone: Small SAC actor-critic network (lidar/goal/waypoint featurizer, Fig. 3), trained from scratch with RL
setting.training_data: RL in simulation: 200,000 training steps with 4 parallel iGibson environments on 3–4 simple WALLS- layouts with ORCA pedestrians (or on a single Gibson mesh scan for the MESH-trained variants); no demonstrations
setting.observation: 1D LiDAR (128 ranges) + goal position in robot frame + 6 global-planner waypoints
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity for a differential-drive robot (v ∈ [-0.2,1] m/s, ω ∈ [-0.5,0.5] rad/s, 0.25 s steps)
setting.simulator: iGibson (PyBullet) with ORCA pedestrians; custom WALLS- layouts and Gibson 3D-scan meshes
setting.privileged: 2D map of static layout and robot localization (used by the global planner to produce waypoints); pedestrians are ORCA agents that see the robot

numbers_note: Only success rate is reported for the CrowdNav circle-crossing test. Only ΠT1 is shown at 16 pedestrians in WALLS-I. Table IV also reports ΠT1 at 4, 6, 8 and 12 pedestrians (SR 98.00 / 95.50 / 88.50 / 88.00; ROS-NAV 90.00 / 77.50 / 74.00 / 70.33). The 4-pedestrian WALLS-I row in Table IV (98.00) differs from Table II (93.50) because it is a separate evaluation. ΠT2 and ΠT3 results are in Table II and were omitted here: ΠT2 SR 92/88/92 and ΠT3 SR 98/94/96 on WALLS-I/H/G. Table III also gives MESH-trained policies on WALLS-H (Π_MESH-MARKET 88.00, Π_MESH-HOME 64.00). The text reports MESH-MARKET in-domain SR as 75% and the average as 79.5%, while Table III prints 75.33. All results are averages over 3 runs × 100 episodes. The benchmarks are the authors' own and non-standard. Training curves appear only in figures.
results: With compositional multi-layout training, ΠT1 averages 95.16% SR on three unseen composed layouts (93.5 / 96 / 96 on WALLS-I/H/G). Single-layout policies drop to as low as 70% (Π_WALLS-F on WALLS-H) and 68% (Π_WALLS-B on WALLS-G), and multi-layout policies missing key elements also drop (ΠT4: 74% on WALLS-I, 78% on WALLS-H). ΠT1 beats the tuned ROS navigation stack (Dijkstra + DWA) at every pedestrian density on WALLS-I: 80.5 vs 62.0 SR at 16 pedestrians, where ROS-NAV's 35% timeouts reflect freezing. It matches SARL's 100% on SARL's circle-crossing domain without training there, and transfers to real 3D scans at 77% (supermarket) and 66% (apartment), versus 79.5% average for mesh-trained in-domain policies, which overfit.
limitations: Evaluation is simulation only. Pedestrians are cooperative ORCA agents that see the robot and follow constrained start/goal areas, so realism of human behavior and real-robot transfer are untested.

Test sets are small and custom (3 walls layouts, 2 mesh scans, 3×100 episodes). ΠT1's failure mode is collisions, which rise sharply with density (19.5% at 16 pedestrians); the paper relies on a separate safety stop for real deployment.
The method assumes a known 2D map and localization for the global planner. Input ablations are claimed without numbers, and no pedestrian prediction or social-norm modelling is included.
builds_on: Deep local trajectory replanning and control (Pokle et al. 2019)
compares_to: ROS navigation stack (Dijkstra global planner + DWA local planner, layered costmaps)
